documents.unit: The Institute for Learning and Teaching (TILT), Academic Integrity
documents.title: NavigateAI Use at CSU: What's allowed, When to ask, and What to avoid
documents.summary: Student-facing CSU Academic Integrity guide using a trail-map metaphor to sort AI uses into open, ask-first, and misconduct, with an FAQ on cheating and plagiarism that defers to the instructor.
documents.stance_why: The page sorts AI use into three zones: always-acceptable learning uses, a permit zone where the instructor decides, and a closed zone of misconduct. Because it sets named tiers and leaves the permit decision to "your instructor" ("Every guide runs their trail differently"), the stance is delegates with tiers rather than one fixed stance.

units.why: The framing sentence sorts uses into "open", "special permits" and "closed" paths; it is a policy because it defines named tiers of AI use, so P05 (tiers) and not P04.
units.anchor: Some paths are open to everyone, some require special permits, and some are closed
units.frag_end: some are closed because the paths are perilous.

units.why: "You are encouraged to use AI as your personal guide for learning and discovery" welcomes AI for learning (not credit) work; it is tutor-like use, so P12 rather than the broader P02.
units.anchor: You are encouraged to use AI as your personal guide for learning and discovery.

units.why: "Use AI to explain a complex topic from class in a new way" is a listed always-acceptable use; explaining class concepts is the tutor use in P12.
units.anchor: Use AI to explain a complex topic from class in a new way.

units.why: Asking AI for key figures or main debates in a field is "always acceptable"; it is exploring concepts like a search engine, matching P12 (P15 is about brainstorming approaches).
units.anchor: Explore concepts related to your course.
units.frag_end: main debates in a scientific field.

units.why: "Create practice questions or flashcards to study for an exam" is an always-acceptable use matching P14 study aids.
units.anchor: Create practice questions or flashcards to study for an exam.

units.why: "AI tools can sometimes lead you astray with wrong information (hallucinations)" states a fact about AI output that grounds the verification duty, so P31 informs.
units.anchor: AI tools can sometimes lead you astray with wrong information (hallucinations).

units.why: "You are always responsible for verifying the facts and the quality of your work" binds students to verify AI output even on open uses, P31 (not P29, which is about owning submissions).
units.anchor: You are always responsible for verifying the facts and the quality of your work.

units.why: "Using AI for any work you get credit for requires their explicit permission" sets a restrict-unless-permitted default; P06 (explicit allowance needed, otherwise not allowed) fits best, not P04 since it is the default itself.
units.anchor: Using AI for any work you get credit for requires their explicit permission.

units.why: "Getting a permit means asking your instructor if, and how, you can use AI for a specific assignment" makes permission assignment-by-assignment, so P04.
units.anchor: asking your instructor if, and how, you can use AI for a specific assignment

units.why: "Every guide runs their trail differently" tells students that instructors set different rules; it is the per-instructor rule setting of P04.
units.anchor: Every guide runs their trail differently.

units.why: Writing or co-authoring graded essays, reports or papers needs instructor sign-off ("Check with your instructor before using AI"); this is a prose rule so P18 over P04.
units.anchor: Write or co-author any part of a graded essay, lab report, or paper.

units.why: Outlining or organizing arguments for a graded assignment needs prior instructor permission; a writing-process rule, so P18.
units.anchor: Outline or organize your arguments for a graded assignment.

units.why: "Generate code or solve problems for credit" is on the check-with-instructor list; AI code is allowed only if the instructor permits, which is P16 (conditional AI code), not P19, since it is not flatly banned.
units.anchor: Generate code or solve problems for credit.

units.why: "Complete any portion of a take-home quiz, exam, or assignment" requires instructor permission; it is a take-home assessment rule decided by the instructor, so P04 rather than P22 (which bans in-class AI).
units.anchor: Complete any portion of a take-home quiz, exam, or assignment.

units.why: "When in doubt, ask your guide" tells students unsure about a use to ask the instructor: P10.
units.anchor: When in doubt, ask your guide.

units.why: "An unauthorized trip here is considered academic misconduct" classifies unpermitted AI use in the permit zone as misconduct: P36.
units.anchor: An unauthorized trip here is considered academic misconduct.

units.why: "Entering it is a violation of CSU's Academic Integrity Policy" ties the closed uses to the integrity policy, so P36.
units.anchor: Entering it is a violation of CSU’s Academic Integrity Policy

units.why: "This applies to anything considered work for credit (graded, pass/fail, or marked as completed)" defines the scope of the prohibitions, P61.
units.anchor: anything considered “work for credit” (graded, pass/fail, or marked as completed)

units.why: Turning in work "fully generated by an AI" is listed as misconduct; it is the core ban on AI producing submitted work, P19 (P36 is the consequence, not the rule).
units.anchor: any other assignment that was fully generated by an AI.

units.why: "Using an AI tool in any way to answer questions during a quiz or exam" is misconduct: no AI on exams, P22.
units.anchor: Using an AI tool in any way to answer questions during a quiz or exam.

units.why: Including "fake sources, data, or citations that an AI made up" is misconduct; the nearest type is P31 (verify AI output, which can be hallucinated).
units.anchor: Including fake sources, data, or citations that an AI made up

units.why: Using AI to "rewrite or spin" source sentences and present them as your own summary is misconduct; a prose-specific rule, P18.
units.anchor: Using AI to rewrite or “spin” sentences or paragraphs from a source

units.why: "Intentionally hiding your use of AI" where disclosure was requested is a violation, making non-disclosure itself the offence: P28.
units.anchor: Intentionally hiding your use of AI on an assignment

units.why: Submitting AI-generated "code, formulas, or solutions" as your own is misconduct; a ban on AI-produced work, with code named, P19.
units.anchor: Submitting AI-generated code, formulas, or solutions and claiming them as your own work

units.why: The helicopter analogy says the assignment goal is "building the strength and skill that only come from the climb": AI shortcuts the practice, P41.
units.anchor: it’s about building the strength and skill that only come from the climb

units.why: Under "How do I credit my AI Tools (when allowed)?" students are sent to the library citation guide; it tells students to cite AI use, P24.
units.anchor: Visit the CSU Library's AI Citation Guide

units.why: The guide discloses that "a large language model" helped brainstorm and refine it; it is the office disclosing its own AI use, P47.
units.anchor: We used a large language model as a collaborative partner to help brainstorm analogies

units.why: The FAQ says who decides acceptable help: "The simple answer is the instructor." That delegates AI-relevant help rules to the instructor, P04.
units.anchor: The simple answer is the instructor.
units.frag_end: The simple answer is the instructor.

units.why: "The expectation can change from course to course" says rules vary by course, so one course's permissions do not carry over: P11.
units.anchor: the expectation can change from course to course
units.frag_end: not allowed to collaborate at all in another.

documents.unit: The Institute for Learning and Teaching (TILT)
documents.title: Crafting Syllabus Statements on Generative Artificial Intelligence Use
documents.summary: TILT guidance for faculty on writing concise AI syllabus statements, with four sample statements and advice on AI literacies. It explicitly leaves the stance to each instructor.
documents.stance_why: The guide says a campus umbrella policy is unlikely and urges instructors to use "best judgment"; it offers four sample statements (prohibitive, conditional, limited, permissive) rather than a rule, so delegates with tiers.

units.why: The guide says "it seems unlikely that a campus umbrella policy will satisfy the many needs", so the decision is left to courses; this is P04 and sets the stance for the whole document.
units.anchor: it seems unlikely that a campus umbrella policy will satisfy the many needs and concerns
units.frag_end: and concerns that have and will arise.

units.why: "They guide: they clarify expectations and help prevent misunderstanding" gives the purpose of syllabus statements; a push to state AI expectations in the syllabus, P09.
units.anchor: they clarify expectations and help prevent misunderstanding

units.why: "When something undesirable occurs... they are what we point to as the stated expectation" says statements back later enforcement; P09 fits as the reason to write them.
units.anchor: they are what we point to as the stated expectation of the course

units.why: "Syllabus statements should aim for clarity and brevity" directs instructors on how to communicate AI rules: P09.
units.anchor: Syllabus statements should aim for

units.why: "Students should immediately understand whether they are allowed to use AI and how" sets the expectation that every statement states the rule: P09.
units.anchor: Students should immediately understand whether they are allowed to use AI

units.why: "An ideal AI syllabus statement should answer four basic questions" (scope, what is permitted or prohibited, framework, next step) tells instructors what the statement must contain: P09.
units.anchor: An ideal AI syllabus statement should answer four basic questions

units.why: "If you plan to use a clarifying resource, a color-coded chart or other guide, reference it here" recommends a color-coded framework, which is P05 (named tiers).
units.anchor: a color-coded chart or other guide, reference it here

units.why: "Encourage dialogue by inviting students to talk with you" has instructors invite questions, the instructor side of P10.
units.anchor: Encourage dialogue by inviting students to talk with you.

units.why: The prohibitive sample says "You may NOT use AI when completing any assignments, assessments, or other work for credit"; a default ban on credit work, P01.
units.anchor: You may NOT use AI when completing any assignments, assessments, or other work for credit

units.why: The same sample says "You MAY use it to investigate, study, summarize, etc. course material"; AI as study aid and tutor, P12.
units.anchor: You MAY use it to investigate, study, summarize, etc. course material

units.why: "Here is a color-coded framework that we will be using to help make this distinction clearer" is a tiered framework tied to the statement: P05.
units.anchor: Here is a color-coded framework that we will be using

units.why: "If you have questions about this policy, come talk to me!" invites students to ask the instructor, P10 (appears in two samples; coded once).
units.anchor: If you have questions about this policy, come talk to me!

units.why: "You may only use generative AI in this class in specific ways" allows AI only for listed uses, a restrict-by-default rule; P06 is the closest type (not allowed unless specified).
units.anchor: You may only use generative AI in this class in specific ways.

units.why: "I will use a color-coded framework to make it clear HOW you can use AI and WHEN" is a tiered scheme (P05).
units.anchor: a color-coded framework to make it clear HOW you can use AI and WHEN

units.why: "We will discuss how you may use AI on each course assignment or assessment at the time it is introduced" sets the rule per assignment: P04.
units.anchor: we will discuss how you may use AI on each course assignment or assessment
units.frag_end: at the time it is introduced.

units.why: "You are not authorized to use artificial intelligence to produce work for this class except on assignments that I have explicitly identified" bans AI unless explicitly allowed: P06.
units.anchor: You are not authorized to use artificial intelligence to produce work for this class

units.why: "On those assignments, you will receive significant guidance on the appropriate use" is an instructor commitment attached to the permitted assignments; assignment-specific rules, P04.
units.anchor: you will receive significant guidance on the appropriate use

units.why: "You may not construe this limited permission as approval to use these technologies in any other facet" keeps permission to the identified assignments: P11.
units.anchor: You may not construe this limited permission as approval to use these technologies

units.why: "The use of generative AI tools is broadly permitted... to help you brainstorm, draft, and revise" is a permissive default: P02.
units.anchor: The use of generative AI tools is broadly permitted in this course

units.why: "you are fully accountable for the final submission" makes students answerable for what they submit: P29.
units.anchor: you are fully accountable for the final submission

units.why: "Fact-check all AI-generated content for accuracy" requires verification of AI output: P31.
units.anchor: Fact-check all AI-generated content for accuracy.

units.why: "Revise all content to ensure it meets assignment requirements and reflects your own understanding" requires submissions to reflect the student's own understanding: P29 (own work).
units.anchor: Revise all content to ensure it meets assignment requirements

units.why: "Cite your use of the AI tool following the guidance in the CSU Library" requires acknowledging AI use: P24.
units.anchor: Cite your use of the AI tool

units.why: "Submitting inaccurate or unedited AI-generated work... will result in a poor grade" states a consequence in advance (a poor grade): P37.
units.anchor: will result in a poor grade

units.why: "Teach students how to use generative AI tools effectively" asks instructors to teach AI use as a skill (functional literacy): P44.
units.anchor: Teach students how to use generative AI tools effectively

units.why: "Encourage students to evaluate AI's strengths, weaknesses, assumptions, and societal impacts" is critical literacy about AI harms and limits; P53 fits better than P44 since the focus is impacts.
units.anchor: evaluate AI’s strengths, weaknesses, assumptions, and societal impacts

units.why: "Guide students to assess when and how to use AI in different contexts" is rhetorical literacy, teaching judgment in using AI: P44.
units.anchor: Guide students to assess when and how to use AI in different contexts

units.why: The guide lists "environmental impact, unevenly distributed access" and integrity as concerns raised by AI; naming harms, P53 (P51 is about providing access).
units.anchor: critical thinking, environmental impact, unevenly distributed access

units.why: "You are urged to use your best judgment and to update your syllabus languages your ideas change" asks instructors to revise their statements over time: P54.
units.anchor: to update your syllabus languages your ideas change

units.why: "Consider consulting the standards of your disciplinary community" advises instructors to learn from others before setting policy: P63.
units.anchor: Consider consulting the standards of your disciplinary community

units.why: The closing question about "higher order thinking and learning" frames the aim of course AI use as protecting learning: P41.
units.anchor: promotes an approach that reflects the higher order thinking

units.why: The further-reading list is offered "to expand their understanding of generative AI and how to prepare their courses": support for faculty learning, P63.
units.anchor: expand their understanding of generative AI and how to prepare their courses

units.why: "This resource was coauthored using generative AI (Ram-GPT)" discloses the office's own AI use in making guidance: P47 (disclosure of staff AI use).
units.anchor: This resource was coauthored using generative AI (Ram-GPT)

notes: Only two university-layer TILT documents were coded (no school/computing docs; course deferred). Syllabus guide samples are template text addressed to students. Fabricated-citation misconduct had no exact type; coded P31.
